set_title: Upper motor neuron signs: Babinski sign, Hoffmann sign, Sustained clonus, Clasp-knife spasticity and Pronator drift
stem: A 66-year-old man has right-sided weakness after a stroke. The examiner strokes the lateral sole of his right foot from heel to ball; the big toe extends and the other toes fan out. The left foot responds with toe flexion.
oneliner: 66M, post-stroke right weakness + sole stroking gives big-toe extension, toes fan → ?

whyNot.B: Hoffmann is thumb flexion in the hand; here the **sole** was stroked
whyNot.C: Clonus is repeated beats after sudden stretch; here the **sole was stroked**
whyNot.D: Clasp-knife is a tone finding on passive stretch; here the **sole was stroked**
whyNot.E: Pronator drift is tested with **outstretched arms**, not by stroking the foot

why: Big-toe extension with fanning on **lateral sole stroking** is the Babinski sign, a corticospinal tract lesion marker. It is normal in infants.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Big toe extends on sole stroking
Corticospinal tract lesion; normal in infants
Repeated beats after quick ankle dorsiflexion
Resistance then sudden give on stretch
Outstretched arm pronates and drifts down

idea.rule: Upgoing big toe on sole stroking = corticospinal tract lesion.
also: Normal in infants under about 2 years

set_title: Upper motor neuron signs: Babinski sign, Hoffmann sign, Sustained clonus, Clasp-knife spasticity and Pronator drift
stem: A 58-year-old woman has sudden right-sided weakness. With her eyes closed and both arms outstretched palms up, the right arm slowly turns palm-down and sinks. Right-sided reflexes are brisk. Finger-to-nose is accurate and sensation is intact.
oneliner: 58F, sudden right weakness + eyes closed, right arm turns palm-down and sinks → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

options.B: Right median nerve entrapment at the wrist
options.C: Dorsal column loss from vitamin B12 deficiency
options.E: Right C6 radiculopathy from disc herniation

whyNot.A: Cerebellar lesions cause dysmetria; her **finger-to-nose is accurate**
whyNot.B: Median entrapment gives hand paresthesias; her **sensation is intact** and reflexes brisk
whyNot.C: Dorsal column loss impairs position sense; her **sensation is intact**
whyNot.E: Radiculopathy lowers reflexes; hers are **brisk** with sudden onset

why: Palm-down sinking of an outstretched arm is pronator drift. The **brisk reflexes and weakness** place the lesion in the contralateral corticospinal tract.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Big toe extends on sole stroking
Corticospinal tract lesion; normal in infants
Repeated beats after quick ankle dorsiflexion
Resistance then sudden give on stretch
Outstretched arm pronates and drifts down

idea.rule: Arm pronates and sinks with eyes closed = contralateral corticospinal lesion.
also: Drift upward suggests parietal or cerebellar cause

set_title: Upper motor neuron signs: Babinski sign, Hoffmann sign, Sustained clonus, Clasp-knife spasticity and Pronator drift
stem: A 62-year-old man has neck pain, clumsy hands and a stiff gait. The examiner holds his middle finger and flicks the fingernail downward; his thumb and index finger flex briskly.
oneliner: 62M, neck pain, clumsy hands + flicked middle fingernail, thumb flexes → ?

whyNot.A: Babinski is toe extension on sole stroking; here the **middle fingernail** was flicked
whyNot.C: Clonus is rhythmic repeated beats; here the **thumb flexes in one brisk movement**
whyNot.D: Clasp-knife needs slow passive limb stretch; here a **fingernail was flicked**
whyNot.E: Pronator drift is tested with **outstretched arms**, not a flicked nail

why: Thumb and index flexion after a **flicked middle fingernail** is the Hoffmann sign, an upper limb marker of cervical corticospinal tract damage, as in myelopathy.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Big toe extends on sole stroking
Corticospinal tract lesion; normal in infants
Repeated beats after quick ankle dorsiflexion
Resistance then sudden give on stretch
Outstretched arm pronates and drifts down

idea.rule: Flicked middle fingernail makes thumb flex = cervical corticospinal lesion.
also: Hand equivalent of the Babinski sign

set_title: Upper motor neuron signs: Babinski sign, Hoffmann sign, Sustained clonus, Clasp-knife spasticity and Pronator drift
stem: A 45-year-old woman has 6 months of progressive leg stiffness. When the examiner briskly flexes her knee, resistance builds and then suddenly gives way. Reflexes are brisk and both toes are upgoing.
oneliner: 45F, progressive leg stiffness + resistance then sudden give, brisk reflexes → ?
ask: Which neuron lesion best explains this finding?

whyNot.A: Lower motor lesions cause flaccidity; she has **brisk reflexes and upgoing toes**
whyNot.B: Junction disease causes fatigable weakness, not tone; her **reflexes are brisk**
whyNot.C: Parkinsonian rigidity is lead-pipe; hers **gives way suddenly** with upgoing toes
whyNot.D: Cerebellar disease lowers tone; she has **resistance then release** and brisk reflexes

why: Resistance that suddenly gives way on rapid stretch is clasp-knife spasticity. With **brisk reflexes and upgoing toes** it signals an upper motor neuron lesion.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Big toe extends on sole stroking
Corticospinal tract lesion; normal in infants
Repeated beats after quick ankle dorsiflexion
Resistance then sudden give on stretch
Outstretched arm pronates and drifts down

idea.rule: Clasp-knife tone plus hyperreflexia plus upgoing toes = upper motor neuron lesion.

set_title: Neck flexion and nerve-root signs: Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign, Lhermitte sign, Lasegue sign (straight leg raise) and Spurling sign
stem: A 6-year-old boy has fever, headache and photophobia. With him supine, the examiner passively flexes his neck and his hips and knees flex involuntarily. CSF shows 2,000 neutrophils/mm3.
oneliner: 6M, fever, headache + neck flexion makes hips and knees flex → ?

whyNot.A: Kernig is pain on knee extension; here **neck flexion** was the trigger
whyNot.B: Lhermitte is an electric shock down the spine; here the **hips and knees flex**
whyNot.D: Straight leg raise tests lumbar roots; here the **neck was flexed**
whyNot.E: Spurling uses neck extension with compression for arm pain; here **hip and knee flexion**

why: Involuntary hip and knee flexion on **passive neck flexion** is the Brudzinski sign. With fever and neutrophilic CSF it shows meningeal irritation from bacterial meningitis.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Knee extension with hip flexed is painful
Neck flexion makes hips and knees flex
Neck flexion sends electric shock down spine
Cervical cord demyelination, e.g. multiple sclerosis
Raising straight leg shoots pain below knee
L5 or S1 radiculopathy from disc herniation
Neck extension, rotation, compression reproduces arm pain

idea.rule: Neck flexion makes hips and knees flex = meningeal irritation.
also: Kernig tests the hamstrings with hip flexed

set_title: Neck flexion and nerve-root signs: Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign, Lhermitte sign, Lasegue sign (straight leg raise) and Spurling sign
stem: A 27-year-old woman who had painful vision loss last year feels brief electric shocks running down her spine into her limbs whenever she bends her neck forward. Neck examination is otherwise normal.
oneliner: 27F, prior optic neuritis + neck flexion triggers shocks down the spine → ?

whyNot.A: Brudzinski is involuntary hip flexion; hers are **electric shocks down the spine**
whyNot.C: Kernig is hamstring pain on knee extension, not **shocks on neck flexion**
whyNot.D: Straight leg raise causes leg pain; hers follows **forward neck flexion**
whyNot.E: Spurling needs neck **extension** with compression and reproduces arm pain

why: Electric shocks down the spine on **neck flexion** are the Lhermitte sign. With prior optic neuritis it points to cervical cord demyelination from multiple sclerosis.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Knee extension with hip flexed is painful
Neck flexion makes hips and knees flex
Neck flexion sends electric shock down spine
Cervical cord demyelination, e.g. multiple sclerosis
Raising straight leg shoots pain below knee
L5 or S1 radiculopathy from disc herniation
Neck extension, rotation, compression reproduces arm pain

idea.rule: Shock down the spine on neck flexion = cervical cord demyelination.
also: Also seen with B12 deficiency or cord compression

set_title: Neck flexion and nerve-root signs: Kernig sign, Brudzinski sign, Lhermitte sign, Lasegue sign (straight leg raise) and Spurling sign
stem: A 52-year-old man has neck pain with tingling down the right arm into the thumb and index finger. He is afebrile. When his neck is extended, rotated to the right and pressed downward, the arm pain and tingling are reproduced.
oneliner: 52M, neck pain, arm tingling + neck extension, rotation, compression reproduces it → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

options.A: Median nerve entrapment at the wrist

whyNot.A: Median entrapment is not reproduced by **neck extension and compression**
whyNot.B: Lumbar disease affects the leg; his symptoms are in the **right arm**
whyNot.D: Meningitis causes fever and stiff neck; he is **afebrile** with unilateral arm symptoms
whyNot.E: Demyelination causes bilateral shocks on flexion; his symptoms are **one arm, on extension**

why: Arm pain reproduced by **neck extension, rotation and compression** is the Spurling sign, showing cervical nerve root compression, here C6.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Knee extension with hip flexed is painful
Neck flexion makes hips and knees flex
Neck flexion sends electric shock down spine
Cervical cord demyelination, e.g. multiple sclerosis
Raising straight leg shoots pain below knee
L5 or S1 radiculopathy from disc herniation
Neck extension, rotation, compression reproduces arm pain

idea.rule: Neck extension plus compression reproducing arm pain = cervical radiculopathy.
also: C6 root: thumb and index finger

set_title: Pupil signs: Marcus Gunn pupil, Argyll Robertson pupil, Holmes-Adie tonic pupil, Horner syndrome and Hutchinson pupil
stem: A 26-year-old woman has 3 days of painful loss of vision in the right eye on eye movement. She has no ptosis. In a dim room, when the light swings from the left eye to the right eye, both pupils dilate.
oneliner: 26F, painful right vision loss + swinging light, both pupils dilate → ?

whyNot.B: Argyll Robertson pupils are small and irregular; hers **dilate when light swings** right
whyNot.C: Holmes-Adie pupil is dilated with slow constriction; hers **dilate on the swinging light test**
whyNot.D: Horner syndrome has ptosis and miosis; she has **no ptosis**
whyNot.E: Hutchinson pupil is fixed and dilated; hers **react, then dilate**

why: Dilation when light swings to the affected eye is the Marcus Gunn pupil, a relative afferent defect. **Painful vision loss** suggests optic neuritis, often from multiple sclerosis.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Pupils dilate when light swings to affected eye
Small pupils accommodate, don't react to light
Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis on one side
Sympathetic chain lesion, e.g. Pancoast tumor
Fixed dilated pupil on side of mass

idea.rule: Pupils dilate when light swings to the bad eye = afferent defect.
also: Classic cause: optic neuritis in MS

set_title: Pupil signs: Marcus Gunn pupil, Argyll Robertson pupil, Holmes-Adie tonic pupil, Horner syndrome and Hutchinson pupil
stem: A 61-year-old smoker has 2 months of left shoulder and arm pain. His left upper eyelid droops, the left pupil is smaller than the right and reacts to light, and the left side of his face does not sweat.
oneliner: 61M smoker, left shoulder pain + ptosis, miosis, left facial anhidrosis → ?
ask: Where is the lesion most likely?

options.A: Oculomotor nerve in the cavernous sinus
options.B: Left optic nerve from demyelinating neuritis
options.C: Sympathetic chain at the lung apex
options.D: Ciliary ganglion after a viral illness
options.E: Dorsal midbrain from a pineal tumor

whyNot.A: Oculomotor palsy dilates the pupil; his pupil is **small**
whyNot.B: Optic neuropathy does not cause **ptosis and facial anhidrosis**
whyNot.D: Ciliary ganglion damage dilates the pupil; his is **small with facial anhidrosis**
whyNot.E: Dorsal midbrain lesions cause upgaze palsy; he has **ptosis and anhidrosis**

answer: Sympathetic chain at the lung apex
why: Ptosis, miosis and **ipsilateral facial anhidrosis** form Horner syndrome from sympathetic interruption. With shoulder pain in a smoker, suspect a Pancoast tumor at the lung apex.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Pupils dilate when light swings to affected eye
Small pupils accommodate, don't react to light
Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis on one side
Sympathetic chain lesion, e.g. Pancoast tumor
Fixed dilated pupil on side of mass

idea.rule: Ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis = sympathetic lesion; smoker means Pancoast tumor.
also: Also seen with carotid artery dissection

set_title: Pupil signs: Marcus Gunn pupil, Argyll Robertson pupil, Holmes-Adie tonic pupil, Horner syndrome and Hutchinson pupil
stem: A 30-year-old man hit his head in a motorcycle crash. After brief recovery he becomes drowsy. His right pupil is fixed and dilated with the eye deviated down and out. CT shows a lens-shaped right-sided hematoma.
oneliner: 30M, head injury, drowsy + fixed dilated right pupil, eye down and out → ?
ask: Which mechanism best explains this sign?

options.B: Optic nerve avulsion at the canal
options.C: Sympathetic chain disruption in the neck
options.D: Ciliary ganglion damage from viral illness
options.E: Abducens nerve stretch at the petrous apex

whyNot.B: Optic nerve damage causes blindness, not an eye **down and out**
whyNot.C: Sympathetic loss gives a small pupil; his is **fixed and dilated**
whyNot.D: Ciliary ganglion damage is sluggish; he has **drowsiness and eye down and out**
whyNot.E: Abducens palsy deviates the eye medially; his eye is **down and out**

why: A fixed, dilated pupil with an eye **down and out** after head trauma is a Hutchinson pupil: uncal herniation compresses the oculomotor nerve on the side of the mass.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Pupils dilate when light swings to affected eye
Small pupils accommodate, don't react to light
Ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis on one side
Sympathetic chain lesion, e.g. Pancoast tumor
Fixed dilated pupil on side of mass

idea.rule: Fixed dilated pupil on the side of the mass = uncal herniation, CN III.
also: Parasympathetic fibers lie on the nerve surface

set_title: Eye movement signs: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia, Parinaud syndrome, Doll's eye (oculocephalic) reflex, Bielschowsky head tilt and Down-and-out eye
stem: A 29-year-old woman has 3 weeks of double vision on looking left. On leftward gaze her right eye does not adduct, and her left eye shows nystagmus. Both eyes converge normally. She had optic neuritis last year.
oneliner: 29F, prior optic neuritis + on left gaze right eye fails to adduct, converges → ?

whyNot.A: Parinaud is vertical gaze palsy; hers is **impaired adduction on horizontal gaze**
whyNot.B: The oculocephalic reflex is tested in coma; she is **awake with impaired adduction**
whyNot.C: Head tilt eases vertical double vision; hers is **horizontal with failed adduction**
whyNot.E: Oculomotor palsy also loses convergence; hers **converge normally**

why: Failed adduction with **intact convergence** and nystagmus in the other eye is internuclear ophthalmoplegia, from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion, classically multiple sclerosis in the young.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Eye fails to adduct; other eye nystagmus
MLF lesion, multiple sclerosis in young
Eyes move opposite to head turn
Head tilts away from weak eye
Eye rests down and out, ptosis

idea.rule: Failed adduction, normal convergence, contralateral nystagmus = MLF lesion.
also: Named for the side that fails to adduct

set_title: Eye movement signs: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia, Parinaud syndrome, Doll's eye (oculocephalic) reflex, Bielschowsky head tilt and Down-and-out eye
stem: A 17-year-old boy has headaches and vomiting. He cannot look upward. His pupils constrict to a near object but barely to light. MRI shows a mass at the posterior third ventricle with hydrocephalus.
oneliner: 17M, headache, vomiting + cannot look up, pupils react to near not light → ?

whyNot.A: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia impairs adduction; his problem is **vertical upgaze**
whyNot.C: The oculocephalic reflex is tested in coma; he is **awake with upgaze palsy**
whyNot.D: Head tilt eases vertical diplopia; he has **upgaze palsy with light-near dissociation**
whyNot.E: Oculomotor palsy gives ptosis and a down-and-out eye; he has **isolated upgaze palsy**

why: Upgaze palsy with **light-near dissociation** is Parinaud syndrome, from dorsal midbrain compression, here by a pineal region tumor causing hydrocephalus.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Eye fails to adduct; other eye nystagmus
MLF lesion, multiple sclerosis in young
Eyes move opposite to head turn
Head tilts away from weak eye
Eye rests down and out, ptosis

idea.rule: Upgaze palsy plus light-near dissociation = dorsal midbrain compression.
also: Pineal tumor is the classic cause

set_title: Eye movement signs: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia, Parinaud syndrome, Doll's eye (oculocephalic) reflex, Bielschowsky head tilt and Down-and-out eye
stem: A 24-year-old man has vertical double vision after a motorcycle crash. It is worst when he looks down, such as walking down stairs. His left eye sits higher than the right, and he tilts his head to the right. There is no ptosis.
oneliner: 24M, vertical diplopia after crash + worst on down gaze, tilts head right → ?

whyNot.A: Oculomotor palsy causes ptosis and a down-and-out eye; he has **no ptosis**
whyNot.B: Abducens palsy gives horizontal diplopia; his is **vertical**
whyNot.C: Optic nerve injury causes visual loss; he has **double vision on down gaze**
whyNot.D: Trigeminal injury causes facial numbness, not **vertical diplopia with head tilt**

why: Vertical diplopia on down gaze relieved by a **head tilt away from the affected eye** is the Bielschowsky head tilt, a trochlear nerve palsy of the superior oblique.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Eye fails to adduct; other eye nystagmus
MLF lesion, multiple sclerosis in young
Eyes move opposite to head turn
Head tilts away from weak eye
Eye rests down and out, ptosis

idea.rule: Head tilts away from the weak eye = trochlear nerve palsy.
also: CN IV exits the dorsal midbrain
Longest intracranial course; often injured by trauma

set_title: Eye movement signs: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia, Parinaud syndrome, Doll's eye (oculocephalic) reflex, Bielschowsky head tilt and Down-and-out eye
stem: A 70-year-old man is comatose after a stroke. When the examiner briskly turns his head to the right, his eyes move to the left, keeping their position in space.
oneliner: 70M, comatose + head turned right, eyes move left, keep position in space → ?

whyNot.A: Brainstem death abolishes the response; his **eyes move opposite the head turn**
whyNot.B: Pontine destruction leaves the eyes fixed in the head; his **eyes move**
whyNot.C: Oculomotor palsies fix the eyes and cause ptosis; his **eyes move to the left**
whyNot.E: A seizure focus causes sustained deviation; his eyes **move reflexively with head turning**

why: Eyes that move **opposite to head turning** in a comatose patient are the doll's eye reflex. It means the pontine and midbrain gaze pathways are intact.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Eye fails to adduct; other eye nystagmus
MLF lesion, multiple sclerosis in young
Eyes move opposite to head turn
Head tilts away from weak eye
Eye rests down and out, ptosis

idea.rule: Eyes counter-roll with head turning in coma = intact brainstem.
also: Never test with cervical spine injury

set_title: Hand tests: Tinel sign, Phalen sign, Froment sign, Wartenberg sign and Finkelstein test
stem: A 31-year-old pregnant typist has 3 months of nocturnal tingling in her thumb, index and middle fingers. She holds both wrists fully flexed with the backs of her hands pressed together for 60 seconds, and the tingling returns.
oneliner: 31F pregnant typist, night tingling in 3 fingers + sustained wrist flexion reproduces → ?

whyNot.A: Tinel is tapping over the nerve; here **wrists were held flexed**
whyNot.C: Froment tests paper pinch; here **sustained wrist flexion** reproduced the tingling
whyNot.D: Wartenberg is an abducted little finger; her tingling is in **three radial fingers**
whyNot.E: Finkelstein causes radial wrist pain on ulnar deviation; she has **finger tingling**

why: Tingling reproduced by **60 seconds of full wrist flexion** is the Phalen sign, a provocative test for median nerve compression in carpal tunnel syndrome.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Wrist flexion for 60 s causes tingling
Thumb IP flexes when pinching paper
Ulnar nerve palsy (weak third palmar interosseous)
Ulnar wrist deviation over fisted thumb hurts

idea.rule: Wrist flexion for 60 seconds reproduces tingling = carpal tunnel syndrome.

set_title: Hand tests: Tinel sign, Phalen sign, Froment sign, Wartenberg sign and Finkelstein test
stem: A 27-year-old cyclist has 3 weeks of weak grip in his left hand with no sensory loss. When he pinches a sheet of paper between thumb and index finger and the examiner pulls, the tip of his thumb flexes to hold on.
oneliner: 27M cyclist, weak left grip + thumb tip flexes when pinching paper → ?

whyNot.A: Tinel is tapping over a nerve; here the **thumb tip flexes on paper pinch**
whyNot.B: Phalen is a wrist flexion test; here a **thumb flexes on paper pull**
whyNot.C: Wartenberg is an abducted little finger; here the **thumb tip flexes** on paper pull
whyNot.D: Finkelstein tests wrist tendons for pain; here a **thumb flexes on paper pull**

why: Thumb tip flexion to hold paper is the Froment sign: **weak adductor pollicis** is replaced by flexor pollicis longus. It shows ulnar nerve compression.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Wrist flexion for 60 s causes tingling
Thumb IP flexes when pinching paper
Ulnar nerve palsy (weak third palmar interosseous)
Ulnar wrist deviation over fisted thumb hurts

idea.rule: Thumb IP flexes to pinch paper = weak adductor pollicis, ulnar nerve.
also: Cyclists compress the ulnar nerve at Guyon canal

set_title: Hand tests: Tinel sign, Phalen sign, Froment sign, Wartenberg sign and Finkelstein test
stem: A 45-year-old woman has nocturnal tingling in her thumb, index and middle fingers. When the examiner taps over the volar wrist, tingling shoots into the same fingers.
oneliner: 45F, night tingling in first three fingers + tapping volar wrist reproduces it → ?

whyNot.A: Ulnar compression affects the **ring and little fingers**
whyNot.B: Radial injury gives wrist drop and dorsal numbness; hers is the **first three fingers**
whyNot.D: It supplies the lateral forearm; she has **tingling in the first three fingers**
whyNot.E: It supplies the shoulder; her symptoms are in the **fingers**

why: Tingling on tapping over a nerve is the Tinel sign. Tapping the **volar wrist** with symptoms in the first three fingers shows median nerve entrapment in the carpal tunnel.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Wrist flexion for 60 s causes tingling
Thumb IP flexes when pinching paper
Ulnar nerve palsy (weak third palmar interosseous)
Ulnar wrist deviation over fisted thumb hurts

idea.rule: Tapping the volar wrist reproduces finger tingling = median nerve entrapment.
also: Also used at the elbow for ulnar nerve

set_title: Hand tests: Tinel sign, Phalen sign, Froment sign, Wartenberg sign and Finkelstein test
stem: A 40-year-old man has numbness of his ring and little fingers. When he extends his fingers against a table, the little finger drifts away from the ring finger and he cannot bring it back.
oneliner: 40M, ring and little finger numbness + little finger stays abducted → ?

whyNot.B: Median numbness affects the **first three fingers**
whyNot.C: Radial injury causes wrist drop; he has **ring and little finger numbness**
whyNot.D: It is purely motor; he has **ring and little finger numbness**
whyNot.E: It causes a winged scapula, not an **abducted little finger**

why: A little finger that stays abducted is the Wartenberg sign: **weak third palmar interosseous** muscle. It shows ulnar nerve palsy, with ring and little finger numbness.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Wrist flexion for 60 s causes tingling
Thumb IP flexes when pinching paper
Ulnar nerve palsy (weak third palmar interosseous)
Ulnar wrist deviation over fisted thumb hurts

idea.rule: Abducted little finger = weak palmar interosseous, ulnar nerve palsy.

set_title: Hand and arm postures: Ulnar claw, Hand of benediction, Ape hand, Wrist drop, Waiter's tip and Total claw hand
stem: A 42-year-old man had a left humeral shaft fracture treated with a cast 6 weeks ago. When he holds out his arm, his hand hangs limp and he cannot extend his fingers or lift the hand. Shoulder movement and thumb pinch are normal.
oneliner: 42M, humeral shaft fracture + hand hangs limp, cannot extend fingers → ?

whyNot.A: Ulnar claw is ring and little fingers clawed; his **whole hand hangs limp**
whyNot.B: Benediction fails index and middle finger flexion; his **wrist and fingers cannot extend**
whyNot.C: Ape hand loses thumb opposition; his **thumb pinch is normal**
whyNot.D: Waiter's tip involves the shoulder; his **shoulder movement is normal**

why: Inability to extend the hand and fingers after a **humeral shaft fracture** is wrist drop from radial nerve injury in the spiral groove.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Ring, little fingers clawed at rest
Distal ulnar nerve lesion (hook of hamate)
Index, middle cannot flex on making fist
Arm adducted, internally rotated, wrist flexed

idea.rule: Cannot extend wrist and fingers = radial nerve injury in spiral groove.
also: Triceps may be spared if injury is distal

set_title: Hand and arm postures: Ulnar claw, Hand of benediction, Ape hand, Wrist drop, Waiter's tip and Total claw hand
stem: A 4.1-kg newborn delivered after shoulder dystocia holds the right arm against the side, internally rotated, with the forearm pronated and the wrist flexed. The grasp reflex is present and the hand moves normally.
oneliner: Newborn after shoulder dystocia + arm adducted, internally rotated, wrist flexed → ?

whyNot.A: Total claw hand is a paralyzed clawed hand; here the **grasp reflex is present**
whyNot.B: Wrist drop is failed hand extension; here the **shoulder is adducted and rotated**
whyNot.D: Ape hand is thumb opposition loss; here the **arm is adducted and rotated**
whyNot.E: Ulnar claw affects the ring and little fingers; the **hand moves normally**

why: An adducted, internally rotated arm with flexed wrist after **shoulder dystocia** is the waiter's tip posture of Erb palsy, an upper trunk (C5-C6) injury.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Ring, little fingers clawed at rest
Distal ulnar nerve lesion (hook of hamate)
Index, middle cannot flex on making fist
Arm adducted, internally rotated, wrist flexed

idea.rule: Adducted, internally rotated arm after dystocia = upper trunk (C5-C6) injury.

set_title: Hand and arm postures: Ulnar claw, Hand of benediction, Ape hand, Wrist drop, Waiter's tip and Total claw hand
stem: A 7-year-old boy fell on his outstretched arm and has a supracondylar humerus fracture. When he tries to make a fist, his index and middle fingers stay extended and his thumb flexes weakly.
oneliner: 7M, supracondylar fracture + trying a fist, index and middle fingers stay straight → ?

whyNot.B: Ulnar injury claws ring and little fingers; his **index and middle fingers** fail
whyNot.C: Radial injury causes wrist drop; his **index and middle fingers fail to flex**
whyNot.D: It supplies the deltoid and teres minor; his deficit is in the **hand**
whyNot.E: It supplies elbow flexors; his deficit is **finger and thumb flexion**

why: Index and middle fingers that stay straight on attempted fist are the hand of benediction, showing **proximal median nerve injury**, as in supracondylar fracture.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Ring, little fingers clawed at rest
Distal ulnar nerve lesion (hook of hamate)
Index, middle cannot flex on making fist
Arm adducted, internally rotated, wrist flexed

idea.rule: Index and middle fingers stay straight on fist = proximal median nerve lesion.

set_title: Hand and arm postures: Ulnar claw, Hand of benediction, Ape hand, Wrist drop, Waiter's tip and Total claw hand
stem: A 28-year-old man fell onto the heel of his hand, fracturing the hook of the hamate. At rest his ring and little fingers are hyperextended at the knuckles and flexed at the finger joints. Thumb opposition is normal.
oneliner: 28M, hook of hamate fracture + ring and little fingers clawed at rest → ?

whyNot.A: Median injury impairs thumb opposition; his **thumb opposition is normal**
whyNot.B: Radial injury causes wrist drop, not **clawed ring and little fingers**
whyNot.C: It supplies elbow flexors; his deficit is **clawed ring and little fingers**
whyNot.E: It supplies serratus anterior; his deficit is in the **hand**

why: Clawed ring and little fingers at rest are the ulnar claw: **lost lumbricals** let extensors and flexors overpull. The lesion is of the ulnar nerve.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Ring, little fingers clawed at rest
Distal ulnar nerve lesion (hook of hamate)
Index, middle cannot flex on making fist
Arm adducted, internally rotated, wrist flexed

idea.rule: Ring and little fingers clawed = ulnar nerve lesion, lumbricals lost.
also: Distal lesions claw more than proximal

set_title: Gait signs: Romberg sign, Steppage gait, Magnetic gait, Festinating gait, Wide-based ataxic gait and Circumduction gait
stem: A 74-year-old man has 6 months of memory loss and urinary incontinence. He takes a long time to start walking, takes short steps as if his feet were stuck to the floor, and turns slowly. He has no tremor.
oneliner: 74M, memory loss, incontinence + feet seem stuck to floor, no tremor → ?

whyNot.B: Romberg is about standing balance with eyes closed; his **feet stick while walking**
whyNot.C: Steppage lifts the knee high; his **feet stay stuck to the floor**
whyNot.D: Festinating has quickening steps and rest tremor; he has **no tremor** and feet stuck
whyNot.E: Ataxia is a broad staggering stance; his steps are **short and stuck**

why: Hesitant start, short steps and feet that seem **stuck to the floor** are a magnetic gait. With incontinence and dementia it indicates normal pressure hydrocephalus.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Falls when eyes close, stable when open
Foot drop, common fibular (peroneal) nerve injury
Short shuffling steps that speed up
Broad stance, staggering, can't tandem walk
Stiff leg swung out in an arc

idea.rule: Feet stuck to floor plus incontinence plus dementia = normal pressure hydrocephalus.

set_title: Gait signs: Romberg sign, Steppage gait, Magnetic gait, Festinating gait, Wide-based ataxic gait and Circumduction gait
stem: A 16-year-old wrestler has right foot drop. When he walks, he lifts his right knee high and slaps the foot down. Ankle dorsiflexion and eversion are weak, with reduced sensation over the lateral lower leg and dorsum of the foot.
oneliner: 16M wrestler, foot drop + high knee lift, weak dorsiflexion and eversion → ?

whyNot.A: Tibial injury weakens plantar flexion; his **dorsiflexion and eversion** are weak
whyNot.B: Femoral injury weakens knee extension; his deficit is **foot drop with eversion weakness**
whyNot.C: Obturator injury weakens thigh adduction; his deficit is **dorsiflexion and eversion**
whyNot.E: Superior gluteal injury causes a pelvic tilt; his deficit is **foot drop**

why: A high-stepping gait with foot slap is steppage gait from foot drop. Weak **dorsiflexion and eversion** with lateral leg numbness localize to the common fibular nerve at the fibular neck.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Falls when eyes close, stable when open
Foot drop, common fibular (peroneal) nerve injury
Short shuffling steps that speed up
Broad stance, staggering, can't tandem walk
Stiff leg swung out in an arc

idea.rule: High-stepping foot drop = common fibular nerve injury at fibular neck.

set_title: Gait signs: Romberg sign, Steppage gait, Magnetic gait, Festinating gait, Wide-based ataxic gait and Circumduction gait
stem: A 55-year-old man with 20 years of heavy alcohol use walks with a broad stance and staggers. He sways equally with eyes open or closed and cannot tandem walk. Finger-to-nose testing and speech are normal.
oneliner: 55M, chronic alcohol use + broad staggering stance, normal finger-to-nose → ?

options.C: Dorsal columns of the spinal cord

whyNot.A: Hemisphere lesions cause limb ataxia; his **finger-to-nose is normal**
whyNot.C: Dorsal column loss worsens with eyes closed; he sways **equally with eyes open**
whyNot.D: Nigral loss causes shuffling and rest tremor, not a **broad staggering stance**
whyNot.E: Frontal lesions cause hesitant stuck feet; he **staggers with a broad stance**

why: A broad, staggering stance with **normal limb coordination** is a wide-based ataxic gait, from midline cerebellar vermis damage, classically alcohol-related.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Falls when eyes close, stable when open
Foot drop, common fibular (peroneal) nerve injury
Short shuffling steps that speed up
Broad stance, staggering, can't tandem walk
Stiff leg swung out in an arc

idea.rule: Truncal and gait ataxia, spared limbs = cerebellar vermis lesion.

set_title: Head trauma signs: Battle sign, Raccoon eyes, Halo sign, Hemotympanum and Lucid interval
stem: A 34-year-old man fell from a ladder 2 days ago. He now has ecchymosis behind the right ear over the mastoid process. There is no scalp laceration and no drainage from the nose or ear.
oneliner: 34M, fall 2 days ago + bruising behind the right ear over mastoid → ?

whyNot.A: Raccoon eyes are periorbital bruising; here the bruise is **behind the ear**
whyNot.B: The halo sign needs bloody drainage on gauze; he has **no drainage**
whyNot.C: Hemotympanum is blood behind the eardrum; his bruise is **external**
whyNot.D: A lucid interval is recovery then decline; he has **a mastoid bruise**

why: Delayed bruising over the **mastoid** is the Battle sign, indicating a basilar skull fracture of the middle cranial fossa.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Bruising behind the ear over mastoid
Bloody drip forms clear outer ring
CSF leak from basilar skull fracture

idea.rule: Mastoid bruising after head trauma = middle fossa basilar skull fracture.
also: Appears hours to days after injury

set_title: Head trauma signs: Battle sign, Raccoon eyes, Halo sign, Hemotympanum and Lucid interval
stem: A 22-year-old man has bloody fluid dripping from his nose after a motorcycle crash. When a drop falls on gauze, a central blood spot forms with a clear ring spreading around it.
oneliner: 22M, crash + bloody nasal drip on gauze forms central spot with clear ring → ?

whyNot.A: Battle sign is mastoid bruising; here the finding is **a drip on gauze**
whyNot.B: Raccoon eyes are periorbital bruising; here the finding is **a ring on gauze**
whyNot.D: Hemotympanum is blood behind the eardrum; here **nasal fluid forms a ring**
whyNot.E: A lucid interval is a time course; here **gauze shows a clear ring**

why: A **clear ring around a bloody drip** is the halo sign, showing CSF mixed with blood from a basilar skull fracture, here with rhinorrhea.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Bruising behind the ear over mastoid
Bloody drip forms clear outer ring
CSF leak from basilar skull fracture

idea.rule: Clear ring around bloody drip = CSF leak from basilar skull fracture.

set_title: Head trauma signs: Battle sign, Raccoon eyes, Halo sign, Hemotympanum and Lucid interval
stem: A 28-year-old unhelmeted motorcyclist has had 1 day of bilateral periorbital bruising. Eye movements and visual acuity are normal, and he has no direct blow to the orbits.
oneliner: 28M, crash + bilateral periorbital bruising, normal eye movements → ?
ask: Which injury best explains this sign?

options.D: Nasal bone fracture with septal hematoma

whyNot.A: Middle fossa fractures bruise behind the ear; his bruising is **periorbital**
whyNot.C: Blowout gives unilateral enophthalmos and restricted upgaze; his **eye movements are normal**
whyNot.D: Nasal fracture bruises the nose; his bruising is **bilateral periorbital with no orbital blow**
whyNot.E: Epidural hematoma is intracranial; it does not cause **bilateral periorbital bruising**

why: Bilateral periorbital bruising without orbital trauma is raccoon eyes, from blood tracking out of an **anterior cranial fossa** basilar skull fracture.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Bruising behind the ear over mastoid
Bloody drip forms clear outer ring
CSF leak from basilar skull fracture

idea.rule: Periorbital bruising without orbital blow = anterior fossa basilar fracture.

set_title: Head trauma signs: Battle sign, Raccoon eyes, Halo sign, Hemotympanum and Lucid interval
stem: A 15-year-old boy is struck on the right temple by a baseball and briefly loses consciousness. He then talks normally for an hour before becoming drowsy with a dilated right pupil. CT shows a lens-shaped collection.
oneliner: 15M, temple blow + brief knockout, normal hour, then drowsy; CT lens-shaped → ?

options.A: Bridging veins crossing the subdural space

whyNot.A: Bridging veins cause a crescent-shaped bleed; his CT shows a **lens-shaped collection**
whyNot.B: Ruptured aneurysm gives thunderclap headache; his decline followed a **temporal blow**
whyNot.C: A sinus tear bleeds at the midline; his blow was **temporal, lens-shaped collection**
whyNot.D: Hypertensive deep bleeds occur in older adults; he is **15 with trauma**

why: A brief recovery before rapid decline after a temporal blow is the lucid interval of an **epidural hematoma**, from a torn middle meningeal artery.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Bruising behind the ear over mastoid
Bloody drip forms clear outer ring
CSF leak from basilar skull fracture

idea.rule: Lucid interval after temporal trauma = middle meningeal artery bleed.
also: Fracture of the pterion tears the artery

set_title: Named triads I: Charcot triad, Reynolds pentad, Virchow triad, Whipple triad and Cushing triad
stem: A 29-year-old man has a severe head injury. His BP rises to 190/100 mm Hg from 120/80, heart rate falls to 48/min, and respirations become irregular.
oneliner: 29M, severe head injury + BP 190/100, HR 48, irregular respirations → ?

options.A: Neurogenic shock from spinal cord injury

whyNot.A: Neurogenic shock causes hypotension; his BP is **190/100**
whyNot.B: Hypovolemia causes hypotension and tachycardia; he has **BP 190/100 and HR 48**
whyNot.D: Tamponade causes hypotension and tachycardia; he has **BP 190/100 and HR 48**
whyNot.E: Thyroid storm causes tachycardia and fever; his **heart rate is 48**

why: Hypertension, **bradycardia** and irregular breathing are the Cushing triad: the brain is being squeezed, so raised intracranial pressure threatens herniation.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Low glucose, symptoms, relief with glucose

idea.rule: Hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing = raised intracranial pressure.

set_title: Named triads II: Wernicke triad, Hakim triad, Plummer-Vinson triad, Meigs syndrome and Kartagener triad
stem: A 55-year-old woman with chronic alcohol use and poor diet is confused, staggers with a broad-based gait, and has nystagmus with lateral gaze palsy. She has no incontinence.
oneliner: 55F, chronic alcohol use + confusion, staggering gait, nystagmus, gaze palsy → ?

whyNot.B: Hakim triad includes incontinence; she has **nystagmus and gaze palsy, no incontinence**
whyNot.C: Plummer-Vinson has dysphagia and webs; she has **ophthalmoplegia and ataxia**
whyNot.D: Meigs syndrome is fibroma, ascites, effusion; she has **ocular signs and confusion**
whyNot.E: Kartagener triad is situs inversus and sinusitis; she has **gaze palsy and ataxia**

why: Confusion, ataxia and **ophthalmoplegia** are the Wernicke triad of thiamine deficiency. Give thiamine before glucose in alcohol use disorder.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Dysphagia, esophageal webs, iron deficiency anemia
Iron deficiency; raises esophageal SCC risk
Ovarian fibroma, ascites, right pleural effusion

idea.rule: Confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia = thiamine deficiency.
also: Mammillary bodies atrophy in Korsakoff syndrome

set_title: Named triads II: Wernicke triad, Hakim triad, Plummer-Vinson triad, Meigs syndrome and Kartagener triad
stem: A 72-year-old man has had 6 months of urinary incontinence, forgetfulness and a slow, shuffling walk. CT shows enlarged ventricles without cortical atrophy, and lumbar puncture opening pressure is normal. Eye movements are normal.
oneliner: 72M, incontinence, forgetfulness, shuffling walk, enlarged ventricles → ?

whyNot.A: Wernicke triad includes ophthalmoplegia; his **eye movements are normal**
whyNot.B: Plummer-Vinson has dysphagia and webs; he has **incontinence and enlarged ventricles**
whyNot.C: Meigs syndrome occurs in women with ovarian fibroma; he has **enlarged ventricles**
whyNot.E: Kartagener triad is situs inversus and sinusitis; he has **incontinence and enlarged ventricles**

why: Urinary incontinence, gait apraxia and dementia with **enlarged ventricles** form the Hakim triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Dysphagia, esophageal webs, iron deficiency anemia
Iron deficiency; raises esophageal SCC risk
Ovarian fibroma, ascites, right pleural effusion

idea.rule: Incontinence, gait disturbance, dementia = normal pressure hydrocephalus.

set_title: Muscle and calcium signs: Chvostek sign, Trousseau sign of hypocalcemia, Gowers sign, Grip myotonia and Post-exercise facilitation
stem: A 57-year-old woman with a 40-pack-year smoking history has 5 weeks of leg weakness when climbing stairs, dry mouth and constipation. Her knee reflexes are absent at rest but return after she contracts the quadriceps for 10 seconds, and strength improves with repeated effort.
oneliner: 57F, heavy smoker, proximal leg weakness, dry mouth + reflexes return after sustained effort → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Myasthenia worsens with repeated effort; her strength **improves with repeated effort**
whyNot.C: Polymyositis weakness does not improve; hers has **dry mouth and reflexes returning with effort**
whyNot.D: ALS adds upper motor signs; she has **absent reflexes that return after effort**
whyNot.E: Myotonic dystrophy shows slow muscle relaxation; she has **dry mouth and areflexia**

why: Repeated effort lets calcium build up in the nerve terminal and release more acetylcholine. Antibodies block **presynaptic calcium channels**, usually from small cell lung cancer.

idea.rule: Weakness and areflexia that improve with effort in a smoker = Lambert-Eaton.
also: Screen for small cell lung cancer

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Tapping facial nerve twitches the face
BP cuff inflation causes carpal spasm
Climbs hands up legs to stand
Strength and reflexes improve with effort

set_title: Heat and cold triggered signs: Uhthoff phenomenon, Raynaud phenomenon, Ice pack test, Cold-induced acrocyanosis and Ice cube test
stem: A 31-year-old woman who had optic neuritis 2 years ago develops blurred vision and leg weakness while in a hot shower. Her symptoms resolve within 30 minutes of cooling down. MRI shows periventricular white matter lesions.
oneliner: 31F, prior optic neuritis + blurred vision and leg weakness in a hot shower → ?

whyNot.A: Raynaud is colour change from cold; her symptoms came with **a hot shower**
whyNot.B: The ice pack test is cold easing ptosis; hers is **heat-triggered**
whyNot.C: Acrocyanosis is cold-triggered blue digits; her trigger was **heat**
whyNot.E: The ice cube test raises a cold wheal; hers is **heat-triggered**

why: Heat further slows conduction in demyelinated axons, so old deficits flare briefly. A **prior optic neuritis** and periventricular lesions indicate multiple sclerosis.

idea.rule: Heat worsens old neurologic symptoms, reversible with cooling = Uhthoff, multiple sclerosis.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Heat or exercise worsens neurologic symptoms
Fingers white, blue, then red with cold
Blue fingertips and ears in cold
Ice on skin raises a wheal

set_title: Heat and cold triggered signs: Uhthoff phenomenon, Raynaud phenomenon, Ice pack test, Cold-induced acrocyanosis and Ice cube test
stem: A 28-year-old woman has a drooping right eyelid and double vision that worsen by evening. Ice placed on the closed eyelid for 2 minutes improves the ptosis by 3 mm (positive ice pack test).
oneliner: 28F, evening ptosis and diplopia + ptosis improves after 2 minutes of ice → ?
ask: Which disorder best explains this sign?

whyNot.B: Horner adds miosis and is fixed; hers **fluctuates with evening diplopia**
whyNot.C: Third nerve palsy is fixed; her ptosis **improves with ice and varies by evening**
whyNot.D: Lambert-Eaton rarely causes ptosis and improves with effort; hers **worsens by evening**
whyNot.E: CPEO is slowly progressive and fixed; hers **fluctuates and improves with ice**

why: Cooling slows acetylcholinesterase, so more acetylcholine reaches the receptors. **Fatigable ptosis with diplopia** reflects antibodies against postsynaptic receptors.

idea.rule: Fatigable ptosis that improves with ice = myasthenia gravis.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Heat or exercise worsens neurologic symptoms
Fingers white, blue, then red with cold
Blue fingertips and ears in cold
Ice on skin raises a wheal

set_title: Abnormal movements: Asterixis, Cogwheel rigidity, Chorea, Hemiballismus, Intention tremor and Startle myoclonus
stem: A 66-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension suddenly develops continuous wild flinging of her right limbs. Her mental status is normal and she has no weakness or sensory loss.
oneliner: 66F, diabetes + sudden wild flinging of right limbs, no weakness → ?

whyNot.A: Asterixis is small wrist flapping; hers is **wild flinging of a whole limb**
whyNot.B: Cogwheel is ratchet resistance to passive movement; hers is **spontaneous flinging**
whyNot.D: Chorea is small, random, dance-like jerks; hers are **large flinging movements of one side**
whyNot.E: Startle myoclonus follows noise; hers is **continuous and not provoked**

why: A small lacunar infarct in the contralateral subthalamic nucleus releases motor thalamus from inhibition. **Sudden onset with diabetes and hypertension** fits small-vessel disease.

idea.rule: Sudden flinging of one side = contralateral subthalamic nucleus lesion.

set_title: Abnormal movements: Asterixis, Cogwheel rigidity, Chorea, Hemiballismus, Intention tremor and Startle myoclonus
stem: A 24-year-old man with schizophrenia starts haloperidol. Two weeks later he has a masklike face and ratchet-like resistance when his elbow is moved passively (cogwheel rigidity).
oneliner: 24M, schizophrenia, 2 wk on haloperidol + masklike face, cogwheel rigidity → pathway?
ask: Blockade of which pathway best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Mesolimbic blockade relieves psychosis; it does not cause his **cogwheel rigidity**
whyNot.B: Mesocortical effects are negative symptoms; **cogwheel rigidity** points to the motor pathway
whyNot.C: Tuberoinfundibular blockade raises prolactin; he has **rigidity and a masklike face**
whyNot.D: Corticospinal damage gives spastic clasp-knife tone; his is **ratchet-like on haloperidol**

why: D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway reproduces dopamine loss in Parkinson disease, so **rigidity and a masklike face** follow. Anticholinergics such as benztropine relieve it.

idea.rule: Drug-induced parkinsonism = D2 blockade of the nigrostriatal pathway.

set_title: Abnormal movements: Asterixis, Cogwheel rigidity, Chorea, Hemiballismus, Intention tremor and Startle myoclonus
stem: A 62-year-old man with hypertension has sudden unsteadiness. His right hand is steady at rest but oscillates more widely as it approaches the examiner's finger (intention tremor), and he overshoots the target on the right.
oneliner: 62M, hypertension, sudden unsteadiness + right hand tremor worsening nearing target → lesion?
ask: Where is the lesion that best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Subthalamic lesions cause flinging; his hand **steadies at rest, shakes nearing target**
whyNot.B: Nigral loss causes a resting tremor; his hand is **steady at rest**
whyNot.C: Caudate loss causes chorea; his tremor **worsens nearing the target**
whyNot.E: Motor cortex lesions cause weakness; he has **overshoot on the right**

why: The cerebellar hemisphere corrects limb trajectory, so damage gives overshoot and oscillation that grows near the target. Cerebellar signs appear **on the same side** as the lesion.

idea.rule: Tremor worsening near a target = ipsilateral cerebellar hemisphere lesion.

set_title: Primitive reflexes: Moro reflex, Rooting reflex, Palmar grasp reflex, Galant reflex and Asymmetric tonic neck reflex
stem: A 12-month-old girl born at 28 weeks is not sitting without support. Her legs are stiff with brisk reflexes and scissor on vertical suspension. A finger placed in her palm still produces a strong grasp (palmar grasp reflex).
oneliner: 12-month-old, born at 28 wk, stiff legs, brisk reflexes + persistent palmar grasp → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: SMA causes floppy weakness with absent reflexes; she has **stiff legs and brisk reflexes**
whyNot.B: The grasp should vanish by 6 months; she is **9 months corrected**, spastic
whyNot.D: Duchenne presents later with weakness; she has **spasticity and brisk reflexes**
whyNot.E: Hypothyroidism gives hypotonia and constipation; she has **stiff legs, brisk reflexes**

why: Primitive reflexes persist when upper motor neuron injury delays cortical inhibition. **Prematurity, spasticity and brisk reflexes** at 9 months indicate cerebral palsy.

idea.rule: Primitive reflexes persisting past expected age + spasticity = cerebral palsy.
also: Palmar grasp should go by 6 months

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Arms abduct then adduct when head drops
Turns toward cheek touch, opens mouth
Normal newborn; gone by about 4 months
Fingers close on object in palm
Normal newborn; gone by about 6 months
Back stroke curves trunk toward that side
Head turn extends that arm (fencing posture)
Normal infant; gone by about 6 months

set_title: Neurocutaneous skin and eye signs: Cafe-au-lait macules, Crowe sign, Lisch nodules, Ash-leaf spots, Shagreen patch and Port-wine stain
stem: An 8-month-old boy has clusters of sudden flexion of the trunk and arms. EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. Under a Wood lamp, multiple oval hypopigmented macules are seen on his trunk.
oneliner: 8-month-old boy, infantile spasms + oval pale macules under Wood lamp → ?

whyNot.A: Cafe-au-lait macules are hyperpigmented; his are **pale oval macules**
whyNot.B: Lisch nodules are iris hamartomas; his finding is **skin hypopigmentation**
whyNot.C: Shagreen patch is raised leathery skin; his are **flat pale macules**
whyNot.E: Port-wine stain is purple and facial; his are **pale oval trunk macules**

why: Oval hypopigmented macules are ash-leaf spots, often the earliest skin sign of tuberous sclerosis. **Infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia** fit; look for cardiac rhabdomyoma.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Freckles in the armpits or groin
Leathery orange-peel plaque on lower back
Flat purple facial stain along V1

idea.rule: Pale oval macules + infantile spasms = ash-leaf spots = tuberous sclerosis.

set_title: Neurocutaneous skin and eye signs: Cafe-au-lait macules, Crowe sign, Lisch nodules, Ash-leaf spots, Shagreen patch and Port-wine stain
stem: A 5-month-old girl has focal seizures involving the left arm. Since birth she has had a flat purple-red stain covering her right forehead and upper eyelid (port-wine stain). Her right eye has an elevated intraocular pressure.
oneliner: 5-month-old girl, seizures + flat purple stain over forehead and eyelid → ?
ask: Which condition best explains this sign?

whyNot.A: Tuberous sclerosis has hypopigmented macules and spasms; she has **a purple V1 facial stain**
whyNot.B: NF1 has tan macules and neurofibromas; she has **a purple stain along V1**
whyNot.C: VHL presents in adulthood; she is **5 months old with a facial stain**
whyNot.D: Ataxia-telangiectasia causes ataxia and infections; she has **a facial stain with seizures**

why: A flat purple V1 facial stain with seizures indicates Sturge-Weber syndrome, caused by a somatic **GNAQ** mutation. Leptomeningeal angiomas cause the seizures; glaucoma may accompany.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Freckles in the armpits or groin
Leathery orange-peel plaque on lower back
Flat purple facial stain along V1

idea.rule: V1 port-wine stain + seizures = Sturge-Weber = somatic GNAQ mutation.

set_title: Fundus signs: Cherry-red spot, Hollenhorst plaque, Cotton-wool spots, AV nicking and Blood and thunder fundus
stem: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has sudden painless loss of vision in the right eye. Funduscopy shows a pale, milky white retina; only the fovea keeps its normal color and stands out sharply.
oneliner: 72M, AF + sudden painless monocular blindness, pale retina with contrasting fovea → ?

whyNot.B: Hollenhorst is a yellow arteriolar plaque; his retina is **pale with a contrasting fovea**
whyNot.C: Cotton-wool spots are fluffy patches; his whole retina is **diffusely pale**
whyNot.D: AV nicking is a vessel-crossing change; he has **sudden monocular blindness**
whyNot.E: Blood and thunder shows hemorrhages everywhere; his retina is **pale, not hemorrhagic**

why: A red fovea against a pale retina is the cherry-red spot. The fovea has no inner retina, so the choroid shows through while ischemic retina turns white.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Bright yellow plaque in retinal artery
Widespread hemorrhages, swollen veins, disc edema

idea.rule: Pale retina with red fovea = cherry-red spot; think artery occlusion.
also: Cause here: embolus from the heart

set_title: Fundus signs: Cherry-red spot, Hollenhorst plaque, Cotton-wool spots, AV nicking and Blood and thunder fundus
stem: A 61-year-old man with hypertension has 2 days of painless blurred vision in the left eye. Fundus shows hemorrhages in all four quadrants, dilated tortuous veins and optic disc swelling.
oneliner: 61M, hypertension, painless blurred vision + hemorrhages in all quadrants, swollen veins → ?
ask: Which occlusion best explains this fundus?

whyNot.A: Artery occlusion gives a pale retina; his retina is **full of hemorrhages**
whyNot.B: Branch artery occlusion causes a sector of pallor; he has **all four quadrants involved**
whyNot.C: Ophthalmic artery occlusion causes severe pallor; his fundus shows **hemorrhages and dilated veins**
whyNot.E: Carotid embolism causes transient pallor; his fundus has **dilated veins and hemorrhages**

why: Hemorrhages in every quadrant with swollen veins and disc edema is the blood and thunder fundus of central retinal vein occlusion.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Bright yellow plaque in retinal artery
Widespread hemorrhages, swollen veins, disc edema

idea.rule: Hemorrhages in all quadrants with swollen veins = central retinal vein occlusion.
also: Treat with anti-VEGF for macular edema

set_title: Ear exam findings: Negative Rinne test, Positive Rinne test, Weber lateralizing to affected ear, Weber lateralizing to normal ear and Immobile tympanic membrane
stem: A 58-year-old man has muffled hearing in the left ear after a week of ear fullness. Otoscopy shows dark wax filling the canal. A vibrating tuning fork is heard longer when held on the left mastoid than when held beside the left ear.
oneliner: 58M, muffled left hearing + wax in canal + fork heard longer on mastoid than at ear → ?

whyNot.B: Weber uses a midline fork; this compares **mastoid with air in one ear**
whyNot.C: Weber uses the midline; here **mastoid and air are compared**
whyNot.D: Immobile membrane is seen on otoscopy; here a **fork was tested**
whyNot.E: Positive Rinne has air louder than bone; he hears **bone longer**

why: Bone conduction louder than air conduction is a negative Rinne test, meaning conductive loss in that ear, here from cerumen impaction.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Bone conduction louder than air conduction
Conductive hearing loss in that ear
Air conduction louder than bone conduction
Midline fork louder in the poorer ear
Conductive hearing loss in that ear
Midline fork louder in the good ear
Sensorineural loss in the opposite ear
Eardrum does not move on pneumatic otoscopy

idea.rule: Bone conduction beats air conduction = negative Rinne = conductive loss.
also: Normal: air conduction louder than bone

set_title: Ear exam findings: Negative Rinne test, Positive Rinne test, Weber lateralizing to affected ear, Weber lateralizing to normal ear and Immobile tympanic membrane
stem: A 45-year-old man has hearing loss in the right ear only; the left ear hears normally. A 512-Hz tuning fork placed on the forehead sounds louder in the right ear.
oneliner: 45M, right hearing loss + midline fork louder in right ear → ?
ask: Which type of hearing loss is in the right ear?

whyNot.A: Sensorineural loss in the right ear would **lateralize the fork to the left**
whyNot.C: Presbycusis is sensorineural and bilateral; the fork would **not go to the poorer ear**
whyNot.D: Noise-induced loss is sensorineural; the fork would **lateralize away from the poor ear**
whyNot.E: Meniere disease is sensorineural; the fork would **move to the normal ear**

why: In conductive loss the fork lateralizes to the affected ear: that ear loses room-noise masking, so bone-conducted sound seems louder there.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Bone conduction louder than air conduction
Conductive hearing loss in that ear
Air conduction louder than bone conduction
Midline fork louder in the poorer ear
Conductive hearing loss in that ear
Midline fork louder in the good ear
Sensorineural loss in the opposite ear
Eardrum does not move on pneumatic otoscopy

idea.rule: Weber toward the deaf ear = conductive loss in that ear.
also: Sensorineural loss lateralizes to the good ear

set_title: Ear exam findings: Negative Rinne test, Positive Rinne test, Weber lateralizing to affected ear, Weber lateralizing to normal ear and Immobile tympanic membrane
stem: A 52-year-old man has unilateral tinnitus and hearing loss in the left ear. A 512-Hz tuning fork placed on the forehead sounds louder in the right ear.
oneliner: 52M, left tinnitus and hearing loss + midline fork louder in right ear → ?
ask: Which type of hearing loss is in the left ear?

whyNot.A: Conductive loss would pull the fork **toward the left, deaf ear**
whyNot.B: Otosclerosis is conductive, so the fork would go to the **deaf ear**
whyNot.C: Cerumen impaction is conductive; the fork would **go to the left**
whyNot.E: Perforation causes conductive loss; the fork would **lateralize left**

why: A fork heard louder in the good ear means the affected ear has sensorineural loss, because the damaged cochlea or nerve cannot pick up the bone-conducted sound.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Bone conduction louder than air conduction
Conductive hearing loss in that ear
Air conduction louder than bone conduction
Midline fork louder in the poorer ear
Conductive hearing loss in that ear
Midline fork louder in the good ear
Sensorineural loss in the opposite ear
Eardrum does not move on pneumatic otoscopy

idea.rule: Weber toward the good ear = sensorineural loss in the other ear.
also: Unilateral tinnitus: image for vestibular schwannoma
Rinne stays positive with sensorineural loss

set_title: Breathing patterns: Kussmaul, Cheyne-Stokes, Biot, apneustic and central neurogenic
stem: A 64-year-old man collapses suddenly and does not respond. MRI shows an infarct of the lower pons from basilar artery thrombosis. Each breath is a long, deep inspiration held for several seconds at its peak, followed by a brief exhalation.
oneliner: 64M, lower pontine infarct + long held inspirations, brief exhalations → ?

whyNot.A: Kussmaul breathing is deep, fast and steady; his inspirations are **held for seconds**
whyNot.C: Cheyne-Stokes cycles through crescendo and apnea; each breath **pauses at full inspiration**
whyNot.D: Biot breathing is random and follows medulla damage; his lesion is **lower pons**
whyNot.E: Central neurogenic hyperventilation is fast and sustained; he **holds each inspiration**

why: Breaths that stop at full inspiration are apneustic. Lower pons injury removes the upper pontine signal that switches inspiration off, so inspiration runs on.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Breaths swell, fade, then pause; repeats
Irregular breaths and pauses, no pattern
Lower pons lesion, e.g. basilar stroke
Fast deep breaths without metabolic acidosis

idea.rule: Inspiration held at its peak = apneustic breathing = lower pons lesion.

set_title: Breathing patterns: Kussmaul, Cheyne-Stokes, Biot, apneustic and central neurogenic
stem: A 58-year-old woman with poorly controlled hypertension has a large cerebellar hemorrhage that compresses the brainstem. Her breathing becomes Biot (ataxic) breathing: irregular breaths of varying depth with unpredictable pauses.
oneliner: 58F, cerebellar bleed compressing brainstem + Biot (ataxic) breathing → site?
ask: Damage to which structure best explains this breathing pattern?

options.E: Cervical spinal cord at C3 to C5

whyNot.B: Lower pons damage holds each inspiration; hers are **irregular with unpredictable pauses**
whyNot.C: These lesions cause steady hyperventilation; hers is **irregular with unpredictable pauses**
whyNot.D: Bilateral hemisphere damage gives regular Cheyne-Stokes cycles; her pauses are **unpredictable**
whyNot.E: Phrenic injury weakens the diaphragm; she has **a cerebellar bleed compressing the brainstem**

why: Ataxic breathing has no rhythm because the medullary rhythm generator itself is failing. It warns of impending respiratory arrest.

head: What it is
Classic cause
rows: Breaths swell, fade, then pause; repeats
Irregular breaths and pauses, no pattern
Lower pons lesion, e.g. basilar stroke
Fast deep breaths without metabolic acidosis

idea.rule: Chaotic breathing with random pauses = Biot (ataxic) = failing medulla; arrest is near.
also: Cerebellar bleeds compress the brainstem quickly
